    When will CO2 pass 450 ppm?¶

    EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

    Every month since March 1958, an observatory high on Mauna Loa, a volcano in Hawaii, has measured how much carbon dioxide (CO2) is in the air. It is the longest record of its kind, and its yearly average has gone up every single year. It now stands near 430 parts per million. When will it pass 450?

    To answer, you need a curve that follows the record, and a fair way to tell a curve that has learned the pattern from one that has only memorised the past. Today you fit four curves, choose between them on years they never saw, test the winner once on the most recent years, and read its forecast. Then you see how much that forecast depends on the choice. At home you repeat the method at two more stations, one in the Arctic and one at the South Pole.

    What you'll be able to do¶

    The science. Describe the two patterns in the CO2 record, the long rise and the yearly breath; say when the yearly average reaches 450 ppm by the curve the data choose; and explain why that date is less certain than the fit makes it look.

    The code. A new column made from an old one (a square, a sine, a cosine) · fitting on training months, choosing on validation months, testing once · a loop that compares four models · np.sin, np.cos and np.pi.

    Thirteen places where you write something: nine in class, four at home. Each is headed Your turn, and the cell under it has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes and a comment beside each one saying what goes there.

    The four questions of the class:

    1. What does the CO2 record show?
    2. How do we choose a curve we can trust on years it has not seen?

    Setup¶

    Run the next cell once. It reads NOAA's Mauna Loa file (live if the network is up, the copy stored with the course if not) and the two stations for the homework, which are stored with the course. Then it adds two columns to each table:

    • time: the middle of each month, written as a year with decimals (March 1958 is 1958.21);
    • decades: the time since 1958, counted in decades (2026 is 6.8 decades).

    Counting in decades keeps the numbers small. Later you will square this column and take higher powers of it; counted in years, the fourth power of 2026's value would be about 20 million, far too large for the fit to handle well.

    (The numbers quoted in this notebook come from the stored copy; if your notebook read NOAA's live file, a few may differ in their last digit.)

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# house style, set once, so every plot cell below holds only what matters
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110,
                     "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3, "axes.axisbelow": True})

CACHE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AI4EPS/EPS88_PyEarth/main/data"

def load():
    """NOAA's Mauna Loa monthly CO2 file: live if the network is up, the copy stored with the course if not"""
    # Ask the live archive first. If it is down, or you are offline, read the copy stored with
    # the course instead, so the notebook still runs.
    try:
        return pd.read_csv("https://gml.noaa.gov/webdata/ccgg/trends/co2/co2_mm_mlo.csv", comment="#")
    except Exception as e:
        print("live source unreachable, using the cached copy:", type(e).__name__)
        return pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/" + "week09_co2_mm_mlo.csv")

# mlo, brw and spo are NOAA's codes for the three stations: Mauna Loa, Barrow and the South Pole.
mlo = load()
# Keep the months up to July 2026, the last month in the stored copy, so every notebook gets the same numbers.
mlo = mlo[mlo["decimal date"] < 2026.6]     # NOAA's own time column: July 2026 is 2026.54
mlo["co2"] = mlo["average"]      # each month's average CO2, in parts per million (ppm)
# After Mauna Loa erupted, the months from December 2022 to early July 2023 were measured on
# Maunakea, about 21 miles north. NOAA fills the few months with no measurement by interpolation.

# For the homework: Barrow, Alaska (71° N) and the South Pole (90° S), stored with the course.
# NOAA marks a month with no measurement -999.99; those few months are already removed.
brw = pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/week07_co2_brw.csv")
spo = pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/week07_co2_spo.csv")

for table in [mlo, brw, spo]:
    table["time"] = table["year"] + (table["month"] - 0.5) / 12    # the middle of each month, as a year
    table["decades"] = (table["time"] - 1958) / 10                  # time since 1958, in decades

print("Mauna Loa:", len(mlo), "months, from", mlo["year"].min(), "to", mlo["year"].max())
print("Barrow:", len(brw), "months.  South Pole:", len(spo), "months.")

    1. What does the CO2 record show?¶

    CO2 is counted in parts per million. A reading of 430 ppm means that in every million molecules of air, 430 are carbon dioxide. That is a small share, but CO2 lets sunlight in and holds back some of the heat the ground gives off. It is one of the gases behind the greenhouse effect from the liquid-water week: the difference between the temperature a world would have with no air and the temperature it actually has.

    Where the numbers come from. Charles David Keeling began measuring CO2 on Mauna Loa in March 1958. The observatory sits 3,397 m up the volcano's side, far from cities and forests, so the air it samples has mixed over a wide area; one station there tells you about much of the planet.

    The Mauna Loa Observatory on the volcano's bare lava slope. Photo: Brian Vasel, NOAA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

    Why it rises. Burning coal, oil and gas, and clearing forests, release CO2. About half of what people emit stays in the air (48 percent over 2014–2023, by the Global Carbon Budget 2024); the oceans and the land take up the rest. Carbon is always moving between the air, plants, soils and the ocean; burning fossil fuels adds a flow that had no return path on human time scales.

    The carbon cycle: where carbon is stored (black numbers, billions of tonnes) and how fast it moves (arrows, billions of tonnes a year). The numbers are from the 1990s; today the air holds more, and fossil fuels add more each year. The shape of the cycle is what matters here. Diagram: NASA Earth Observatory, redrawn by Kevin Saff and FischX (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

    How unusual is today's level? Bubbles of old air trapped in the Antarctic ice sheet record CO2 long before anyone measured it. Through the ice ages of the last 800,000 years it swung from below 200 ppm in the coldest times to about 300 in the warmest, and it did not go above 300 until the industrial age:

    CO2 over the last 800,000 years from ice cores, with the last thousand years enlarged; the steep black end is the age of measurements like Mauna Loa's. Figure: Femke Nijsse (CC BY-SA 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

    Two patterns. The first is the long rise, and it is not a straight line: the curve gets steeper as the years go on. The second is a ripple of teeth, one tooth a year. Three years drawn close up show what the teeth are:

    In [5]:

plt.xlabel("month (1 = January)")
plt.ylabel("CO2 (ppm)")

plt.legend()
plt.show()

    Each year CO2 climbs to a high in May and falls to a low in September or October, and each high sits above the last. The yearly fall comes from plants. Most of the world's land that has a winter is in the northern half of the planet: forests and grasslands that green up together in spring and summer, taking CO2 out of the air, and lose their leaves together in autumn and winter, when decay gives it back. Mauna Loa, at 19.5° N, breathes with the north.

    So a curve that follows this record needs two things: a rise that gets steeper, and a ripple that repeats every twelve months. The next section builds one piece at a time, and asks how to tell whether each piece helps.

    2. How do we choose a curve we can trust on years it has not seen?¶

    A curve that fits the past is not yet a curve to trust about the future. A flexible enough curve can pass close to every month in the record and still be wrong about next year, because it has learned the record's accidents along with its pattern. The fair test is to hide some years from the curve and see how well it does on them. In short: hide some data from yourself, then check.

    Three sets, as for an exam. Think of studying:

    • the homework problems are what you learn from;
    • a practice exam tells you whether your way of studying works, and you may change your way of studying after seeing it;
    • the final exam is taken once, at the end. If you took it again and again, changing your answers each time, it would stop measuring what you know.

    A model gets the same three sets of data, here three spans of years:

    • training months, 1958–2000: each curve learns from these;
    • validation months, 2001–2010: years held back to choose between models. Once they have chosen, they are no longer a fair test.
    • test months, 2011 onward: years nobody looks at until the end, checked once, on the model already chosen.

    Why years in order, and not a random third of the months? Because a forecast is about the future. Months picked at random would sit between training months, where any smooth curve does well, and the test would say nothing about years to come. That would be leakage: any route by which information about the data you are scoring on reaches the model before you score it.

    ✏️ Your turn 2¶

    Which months does each set hold?

    Why: every fit and every score below uses these three sets. Each is a mask on the year column, written with the table skills of the tables week.

    1. training: True for the months up to the end of 2000.
    2. validation: True for the months from 2001 to 2010, both years included.
    3. test: True for the months from 2011 on.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: training, validation and test.

    How a curve's miss is measured. As in the age-of-the-universe week: a residual is the data minus what the curve says, one per month, and the root mean squared error (RMSE) sums them up. Square every residual, average the squares, take the square root. The result is a typical miss, in ppm. Here it is always worked out on the validation months, the years the curve did not learn from.

    ✏️ Your turn 3¶

    How badly does a straight line miss the validation years?

    Why: the straight line is the simplest curve, and the one to beat. It is the age-of-the-universe line, with time across instead of distance.

    1. line: a straight line fitted to the training months: decades across (as a one-column table), co2 up.
    2. residuals: the validation months' CO2 minus what the line says for them.
    3. line_validation_rmse: the RMSE of those residuals.
    4. The figure: the line drawn over the whole record.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: line and line_validation_rmse.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    line = LinearRegression().fit(mlo[training][["decades"]], mlo[training]["co2"])
residuals = mlo[validation]["co2"] - line.predict(mlo[validation][["decades"]])
line_validation_rmse = ((residuals ** 2).mean()) ** 0.5
print("the straight line misses the validation months by", round(line_validation_rmse, 2), "ppm")

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(mlo["time"], mlo["co2"], color="0.7", label="data")
plt.plot(mlo["time"], line.predict(mlo[["decades"]]), label="straight line, fitted to 1958-2000")
plt.xlabel("year")
plt.ylabel("CO2 (ppm)")
plt.title("A straight line")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

    The line misses by 7.18 ppm, and the figure shows why: the record curves upward away from it: from 2001 on, almost every month lies above the line.

    A new column lets a line-fitting method draw a curve. In the age-of-the-universe homework you gave the fit a second column, the distance squared. The fit finds one number for each column it is given, so with decades and decades squared it fits

    $$\text{CO2} = a \times \text{decades} + c \times \text{decades}^2 + b$$

    The squared term is small near 1958 and grows fast later, which is exactly the shape of a rise that gets steeper. Nothing else changes: the same fit, the same masks, the same RMSE.

    ✏️ Your turn 4¶

    Does a squared column help on the validation years?

    Why: the record bends upward; a squared column is the simplest way to let the curve bend.

    1. mlo["decades2"]: a new column, the decades column squared.
    2. squared: the curve fitted to the training months with both decades and decades2.
    3. squared_validation_rmse: its miss on the validation months.
    4. The figure: the curve over the whole record.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: squared and squared_validation_rmse.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    mlo["decades2"] = mlo["decades"] ** 2
squared = LinearRegression().fit(mlo[training][["decades", "decades2"]], mlo[training]["co2"])
residuals = mlo[validation]["co2"] - squared.predict(mlo[validation][["decades", "decades2"]])
squared_validation_rmse = ((residuals ** 2).mean()) ** 0.5
print("the squared curve misses the validation months by", round(squared_validation_rmse, 2), "ppm")

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(mlo["time"], mlo["co2"], color="0.7", label="data")
plt.plot(mlo["time"], squared.predict(mlo[["decades", "decades2"]]), label="squared curve, fitted to 1958-2000")
plt.xlabel("year")
plt.ylabel("CO2 (ppm)")
plt.title("A curve with a squared column")

    From 7.18 ppm to 2.2: the bend was most of what the line missed. What is left is mainly the teeth, which neither curve can draw.

    A wave repeats every twelve months, and two columns can draw one. Turn each month into an angle around a circle, one full turn a year: $\text{angle} = 2\pi \times (\text{month} - 0.5) / 12$. (A full turn is $2\pi$; the $-0.5$ puts each month at its middle.) The sine of that angle rises and falls once a year, and so does the cosine, a quarter of a year later. Drawn over twelve months:

plt.plot(month_numbers, np.cos(month_angle), marker="o", label="cosine of the month's angle")
plt.axhline(0, color="0.5", lw=0.8)
plt.ylim(-1.2, 1.7)     # room at the top for the legend
plt.xlabel("month (1 = January)")
plt.ylabel("value")

plt.legend(loc="upper center", ncol=2)

    month_numbers = np.arange(1, 13) month_angle = 2 * np.pi * (month_numbers - 0.5) / 12 plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.5)) plt.plot(month_numbers, np.sin(month_angle), marker="o", label="sine of the month's angle") plt.plot(month_numbers, np.cos(month_angle), marker="o", label="cosine of the month's angle") plt.axhline(0, color="0.5", lw=0.8) plt.ylim(-1.2, 1.7) # room at the top for the legend plt.xlabel("month (1 = January)") plt.ylabel("value") plt.title("Two waves, each one cycle a year") plt.legend(loc="upper center", ncol=2) plt.show()

    The sine is highest in March and April and lowest in September and October; the cosine is highest in December and January and lowest in June and July. Give the fit both, and it chooses how much of each, which lets the mixed wave peak in any month and be any size. Each is a seasonal column: a column that rises and falls once a year, so the fitted curve can rise and fall with the seasons. The curve is now

    $$\text{CO2} = a \times \text{decades} + c \times \text{decades}^2 + s \times \sin(\text{angle}) + k \times \cos(\text{angle}) + b$$

    More columns always fit the training months better. They do not always fit new months better. The squared curve with seasons misses the validation decade by only 0.77 ppm. Why stop there? A cubed column, or a fourth power, would bend the curve more freely and fit 1958–2000 even more closely. The risk has a name, overfitting: a curve that memorises the data you gave it fails on the data you did not. The highest power in a curve is its degree: the degree of a polynomial is how many bends it is allowed: degree 1 is a straight line, degree 2 bends once.

    The way to find out is to try each degree and score it on the validation months. The figure that shows the answer is a validation curve: plot the miss on the training years and on the held-back years against how flexible the curve is; the flexibility worth choosing is where the held-back miss is lowest.

    The two lines tell different stories. On the training months every extra power helps, or at least does no harm: 1.92, 0.97, 0.82 and 0.82 ppm. On the validation months the squared curve wins clearly, 0.77 ppm, and the cubed and fourth-power curves are four to six times worse (4.51 and 3.31). The extra powers let the curve follow small bends in the 1958–2000 record, which buys almost nothing there (from 0.97 to 0.82 ppm), and then carry those bends forward into years where they do not belong: in the figure, the cubed and fourth-power curves fall below the data after 2001. That is overfitting, seen in the data rather than described.

    The two ways to fail have names. Too simple and you miss the pattern; too flexible and you memorise the noise. The line is too simple: it misses the bend everywhere (bias). The cubed and fourth-power curves are too flexible: what they learn depends on the accidents of the years they were given (variance). The squared curve sits between them.

    Think. If you had chosen by the training RMSE alone, which curve would you have picked?

    3. When will CO2 pass 450 ppm?¶

    The validation months have done their job, so now they can join the training months. The choice is made: the squared curve with seasons. Fit it again to everything before the test, 1958–2010, and then, once, see how it does on 2011 onward. That one number is the honest estimate of how well this kind of curve forecasts years it has never seen.

    4. How far can we trust that answer?¶

    2034 is the answer of one curve. Three checks show how much to trust it.

    First: the test misses have a direction. The test RMSE treats a miss above the curve and a miss below it alike. Average the test residuals year by year instead, and see which way they go:

    The curve fitted to 1958–2010 was about right in 2011 (a miss of -0.1 ppm). Since 2016 the real CO2 has been more than 1 ppm above it every year, reaching 3.6 ppm in 2025. The misses did not grow smoothly: they rose in two steps, around 2016 and 2024, and stayed up in between. Fifteen years cannot tell steadily faster bending from two jumps. The curve of Your turn 8 was fitted to every month, so it has already taken those years in; whether the record keeps pulling above it, no fit can say.

plt.xlabel("year")
plt.ylabel("CO2, yearly average (ppm)")
plt.title("Four curves, each fitted to the whole record, read forward")
plt.legend()

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4)) plt.plot(mlo["time"], mlo["co2"], color="0.7", label="data") future["decades3"] = future["decades"] ** 3 future["decades4"] = future["decades"] ** 4 for i in range(4): model = LinearRegression().fit(mlo[candidates[i]], mlo["co2"]) forecast = model.predict(future[candidates[i]]) first_450 = future["year"][forecast >= 450].min() plt.plot(future["year"] + 0.5, forecast, label=f"{names[i]}: 450 ppm in {first_450}") plt.axhline(450, color="black", lw=0.8) plt.xlim(1958, 2060) plt.ylim(300, 560) plt.xlabel("year") plt.ylabel("CO2, yearly average (ppm)") plt.title("Four curves, each fitted to the whole record, read forward") plt.legend() plt.show()

    Inside the record the three curves that can bend lie almost on top of one another; the line, which cannot bend, runs above the data in the middle years and below it at both ends. Beyond the record they spread: the line passes 450 ppm in 2046, the others in 2034, 2034 and 2032, and by 2050 they say anything from 458 to 536 ppm. That is extrapolation: reading a fitted curve beyond the years it was fitted on. Nothing in the data checks it there. The validation decade chose a curve for the ten years after its training data. It says much less about thirty years ahead, and nothing about what people will burn.

    Third: the curve's seasons, as a check of its shape. The fit chose one number for each seasonal column: a weight for the sine and a weight for the cosine. Together they give the curve's yearly wave. If the curve has learned the record, that wave should be about the size and the timing of the teeth you saw in section 1.

    ✏️ Your turn 9¶

    How big is the yearly wave in the chosen curve, and when is it highest?

    Why: the size and timing of the wave are a check the record can answer: the close-up figure of section 1 shows the data's own highs and lows.

    1. sine_weight and cosine_weight: the numbers everything found for sin_month and cos_month. The fit keeps them in .coef_, in the order of columns, so the position of a column's name in columns is the position of its number.
    2. seasonal_part: for the twelve months, sine weight × sine of the angle plus cosine weight × cosine of the angle (month_numbers and month_angle are given).
    3. mlo_swing: the wave's highest value minus its lowest.
    4. mlo_peak and mlo_low: the month numbers where the wave is highest and lowest. np.argmax gives the position of the largest value and np.argmin the position of the smallest, as in the age-of-the-universe week; read the month number at that position from month_numbers.
    5. The figure: the wave over the twelve months.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: mlo_swing, mlo_peak and mlo_low.

    The question, answered¶

    Around 2034, by the curve the validation years chose, fitted to the whole record. Other reasonable curves put the year anywhere from 2032 to 2046, and since 2016 the record has run above the curve fitted to its first 53 years.

    Week 7 summary¶

    The science¶

    When will CO2 pass 450 ppm?
    Choose a model on years it was not fitted to: fit on the training years, choose on the validation years, and test once on years nobody looked at. A model's columns are a choice: a squared column bends the line, a sine and a cosine of the month draw the seasons, and more columns always fit the training years better but can fit new years worse. A forecast beyond the data is an extrapolation: the year CO2 passes 450 ppm moves by more than ten years with the model, and the record has already pulled away from the curve fitted to its first five decades.

    • Leakage. Any route by which information about the data you are scoring on reaches the model before you score it.
    • Polynomial degree. The degree of a polynomial is how many bends it is allowed: degree 1 is a straight line, degree 2 bends once.
    • Overfitting. A curve that memorises the data you gave it fails on the data you did not.
    • Train/test split. Hide some data from yourself, then check.
    • Validation years. Years held back to choose between models. Once they have chosen, they are no longer a fair test.
    • Test years. Years nobody looks at until the end, checked once, on the model already chosen.
    • Seasonal column. A column that rises and falls once a year, so the fitted curve can rise and fall with the seasons.
    • Extrapolation. Reading a fitted curve beyond the years it was fitted on. Nothing in the data checks it there.
    • Bias-variance. Too simple and you miss the pattern; too flexible and you memorise the noise.
    • Validation curve. Plot the miss on the training years and on the held-back years against how flexible the curve is; the flexibility worth choosing is where the held-back miss is lowest.
    • Typical miss. Square every gap between what happened and what the curve said, average the squares, and take the square root: the usual size of a miss, in the data's own units.

    The code¶

    Function What it does
    Python
    for x in things: do the same thing once for each item
    list.append(x) add one item to the end of a list
    list.index(v) the POSITION of value v, so you can read the same position out of another list
    NumPy
    np.cos(x) the cosine of x; with np.sin, a wave that repeats once a year
    np.pi the number pi, 3.14159...: a full turn of a wave is 2 × pi
    np.max(values) / np.min(values) the largest / smallest value of an array or a list
    np.argmax(values) / np.argmin(values) the position of the largest / smallest value, to read the same position out of another array or list
    mask & other_mask True only where both masks are True, the array version of and
    grid[mask] keep only the cells where the mask is True
    np.sin(x) the sine of x, for drawing a wave
    pandas
    table[mask] keep only the rows where the mask is True
    Matplotlib
    plt.plot(x, y) join points with a line — here, the record and each fitted curve
    plt.xlabel / ylabel / title / show label it, then draw it
    plt.bar(positions, heights) one bar per category — the right chart when the bottom axis is a label
    scikit-learn
    LinearRegression().fit(x, y) find one number for each column that gives the smallest total of squared residuals — a line, or a curve when the columns are powers or waves
    model.predict(x) what the fitted line says y should be at each x

    What the numbers mean. Barrow chooses the same curve as Mauna Loa: the squared curve misses its validation decade by 3.23 ppm, against 4.69 for the line and 4.94 and 19.3 for the cubed and fourth-power curves. Every miss is bigger than at Mauna Loa: the Arctic record has bigger teeth and more month-to-month scatter. With these windows the two stations agree on the shape; move the validation decade by five or ten years and Barrow's choice can change, so the agreement is a weak check, not a proof.

    What the numbers mean. Barrow's test miss is 3.84 ppm, against 2.13 at Mauna Loa, and its swing is 14.3 ppm, about two and a half times Mauna Loa's 5.6. Barrow is in the far north, nearer the great forests and tundra of Alaska, Canada and Siberia, the plants that do most of the breathing; by the time air reaches Hawaii it has mixed with air from farther south, and the swing is smaller. The one-wave curve puts its high in March and its low in September; the data's own low comes earlier, in August, because the real yearly wave is not quite a sine.

    ✓ Your turn 12 — the South Pole chooses the cubed curve and swings 1.0 ppm

    What the numbers mean. The South Pole's validation decade chooses the cubed curve (1.65 ppm, against 3.49 for the squared): the choice depends on the station, and a cubed curve chosen on 2001–2010 is a short-range choice, not a law. The swing is only 1.0 ppm, and it is highest in September and lowest in March: six months away from Barrow's. The southern half of the planet has its seasons the other way round, and it has much less land, and so fewer plants to breathe.

    ✏️ Your turn 13¶

    How does the planet's breath change from north to south?

    Why: three stations, three swings. Put them side by side, in order of latitude.

    1. swings: a list of the three swings, Barrow, Mauna Loa, the South Pole, in that order (written at the top of the cell, as Your turns 9, 11 and 12 find them, so a slip there does not cost this part).
    2. The figure: a bar for each station.
    3. biggest: the name of the station with the biggest swing, found with np.argmax.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: swings and biggest.

    ✓ Your turn 13 — the biggest yearly swing is at Barrow (71° N)

    What the numbers mean. The breath shrinks from north to south: 14.3, 5.6 and 1.0 ppm. The long rise goes at about the same pace at all three stations, because CO2 mixes around the whole planet within about a year (the levels differ a little: the north, where most of it is emitted, runs a few ppm above the South Pole); the yearly swing is local, and it is biggest where the northern plants are. These are the one-wave curve's swings. Measured directly from the data they are a little bigger (about 16 ppm at Barrow and 6 at Mauna Loa), because the real yearly wave is not quite a sine.

    The whole planet at once. NOAA samples the air at dozens of sites from pole to pole. Its picture of every latitude together shows what your three stations found: a big yearly swing in the north, a small one in the tropics, almost none in the far south, and one long rise everywhere.
